title: Subbing for Cab Calloway at the Cotton Club and unpaid rehearsals
summary: The Blue Rhythm Band replaced Calloway, and producers called unpaid all-night rehearsals until the union forced pay.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: From the Russell band, you ended up joining the Mills Blue Rhythm Band.

Yeah, whatever... In between there, I was... I had worked with Willie Lynch's band. Willie Lynch, I think, had the first Blue Rhythm Band. And I worked with that band a short while, not too long. We worked in the Cotton Club as a substitute for Cab Calloway's band. Cab Calloway went on the road, and the Blue Rhythm band went to work in the Cotton Club as a substitute for Cab.
So here you are now playing for a Cotton Club show or Cotton Club revue, so to speak.
Now, you must have had to rehearse that with dancers and so on.
So what did you do? Did you rehearse all afternoon?
No, we rehearsed practically all night after we finished work.

I mean, rehearsals wasn't bad. The only thing bad about the rehearsals at that time, they didn't have to pay the musicians to rehearse. So any time a chorus girl would get out there during a show at night and she didn't kick her leg high enough, or she missed a step or something, the producer of the show would call a rehearsal after the night's work was over. I think we got through around three o'clock at the Cotton Club, two or three o'clock in the morning. And they'd keep us, the show and the band, keep us rehearsing until whenever they felt like letting us go home. Sometimes it would be broad daylight when we would come out of there. And we would never get a nickel for that, not five cents, and if you complained too much you'd get fired -- which was not exactly right.

Now, when the union stepped in years later and made these places pay off for these rehearsals and things, it was very strange how quickly the musicians knew all of the music, according to the producers. They actually knew it. There were no more rehearsals called, you know, extemporaneously. When you had a rehearsal, it had to be a rehearsal, and then they had to pay you for the time.
But up until then, your time wasn't worth nothin', and they'd have you rehearsing every night, six or seven o'clock

in the morning, which didn't make sense. You used to go to work in there at seven o'clock in the evening. The show went on... I think we went to work around six o'clock, and played dance music up until the time of the show, and they put on the show at seven o'clock in the evening. And the show would run over an hour. It was a big production. And we would put on three shows a night, three shows a night. I mean, it was a grind. Now, after you put on three shows a night, and then the producer comes around and tells you "Rehearsal"... Rehearsal, after you've worked all those hours, and here comes the producer -- "Rehearsal." Now you rehearse until six and seven o'clock in the morning, there's no telling what time you'll get home, because you're gonna stop before you go home to get something to eat. Oh, it was just rough. And by the time you'd get home and get a little bit of sleep, it's time to go back down there to go to work again!
